items.headline: Baidu's AI cloud sales jump 94% while search ads sink 22%
items.caption: Baidu's Q3 revenue slipped about 1% to 30.8 billion yuan, in line with forecasts. AI cloud nearly offset the drop in ads.
detail: Baidu said third-quarter revenue was 30.81 billion yuan, about $4.62 billion. That is down about 1% from a year ago and matched the average analyst estimate.

The mix is changing fast. AI cloud infrastructure revenue rose 94% to 8.2 billion yuan, and its wider AI-linked businesses grew 37%. Online ad revenue, Baidu's old core, fell 22% to 11.9 billion yuan.
Baidu swung to a net profit of 1.4 billion yuan, after an 11.23 billion yuan loss a year earlier. US-listed shares were down more than 1% before the bell.
money: Watch the mix, not just the total: a company can shrink overall while its growth unit booms.
AI cloud growth in China shows demand for computing is still strong outside the US.
If you own China tech funds, check how much depends on ad revenue that is falling.
risk: Chinese stocks carry policy and US-China trade risk.

items.caption: House Bill 110 would more than double Texas' pay floor. If passed, it would start Sept. 1, 2027.

visual.title: Texas hourly minimum
visual.foot: About $310 more a week before taxes for a 40-hour job

detail: Six Democratic lawmakers filed House Bill 110 and similar measures ahead of Texas' next legislative session. The lead sponsor is state Rep. Ana-María Rodríguez Ramos of Richardson.

The bills would raise the state minimum to $15 an hour from $7.25, the level set in 2009. A full-time worker would earn about $310 more per week before taxes. The state rate could go higher if the federal minimum ever tops $15.
The Legislature meets Jan. 12, 2027. No votes have happened yet, and the bills would take effect Sept. 1, 2027, if passed.

Small employers can model a $15 floor now to plan prices and staffing.

Families with mixed status: keep documents current and know your legal options.

items.headline: HUD rule ends housing aid for mixed-status families starting Dec. 14
items.caption: Every household member must now be a verified citizen or eligible noncitizen. Opponents say about 80,000 people could be displaced.
detail: HUD finalized a rule that requires every member of a household in public housing, Section 8 and other HUD programs to be a verified US citizen or eligible noncitizen. Families can no longer keep ineligible members while getting reduced, prorated aid, an option in place since 1995.

Citizens who once signed a simple declaration may now need documents like a passport or birth certificate. Opponents estimate about 80,000 people in 20,000 households could lose housing. HUD cited an audit finding nearly 200,000 tenants without verified citizenship.
HUD's own analysis puts costs at up to $251 million and projects no savings. Landlords get 90 days after Dec. 14 to comply.
money: Tenants in HUD housing: gather passports or birth certificates for every household member now.
Ask your housing authority about deadlines before the 90-day window closes.
Mixed-status families may need a backup housing budget; local legal aid can help review options.
risk: Paperwork gaps could lead to aid loss even for eligible citizens.
Lawsuits or changes in Congress could alter the rule.

items.headline: Medicaid work rules still start Jan. 1, but states can't cut people off until July 1
items.caption: Federal officials gave states six more months before removing anyone for not meeting the new work rule. States can still act early.
detail: The federal Medicaid agency told states Friday that the new work requirement still takes effect nationwide on Jan. 1. But states can now wait until July 1 to deny or end coverage for people who don't comply. States may still start earlier.

The rule covers adults in the Medicaid expansion adopted by 40 states, mostly lower-income adults without kids at home. Many must work, volunteer or study at least 80 hours a month. People over 64, caregivers of children under 14 and the medically frail are exempt.
States asked for time to build staff and systems. In Nebraska, which started early, 533 people were denied, mostly over paperwork.
money: If you're on Medicaid, start keeping pay stubs or volunteer logs now so you're ready to report hours.
Check if you qualify for an exemption, such as caring for a child under 14.
Answer every state letter fast; most denials so far came from missed paperwork.
risk: Your state may still enforce early, so check your state's own dates.

items.headline: Hollywood studio landlord Hackman faces $2.1B in loan defaults; a Radford auction looms

detail: Culver City-based Hackman Capital Partners, which bought up studio lots from 2018 to 2021, is in financial trouble. Lenders have filed defaults or moved to foreclose on five properties since January, with loans totaling more than $2.1 billion.

Hackman blames the slump in production after the pandemic, the 2023 strikes and shoots moving to cheaper places. Radford Studio Center's 2025 operating income was $15.6 million, versus $60 million projected when its loan was made. Netflix has been under contract since June to buy Radford for close to $400 million.
Some lots are still healthy, including Culver Studios, leased to Amazon, and Raleigh Studios, leased to Netflix.

LA film workers: the slump shows why an emergency fund of several months matters in gig-heavy jobs.

detail: Stellantis agreed to sell its long-idle Brampton, Ontario, assembly plant and equipment to Roshel, a private maker of armored vehicles. The price wasn't disclosed, and the deal should close by the end of 2026, pending government approvals.

Roshel's CEO said the site won't be limited to defense and could take on auto work, but plans depend on contracts. Canada and NATO allies agreed to raise defense spending to 5% of GDP by 2035, and Roshel wants more capacity. Questions remain about how many jobs the site will bring back.

items.headline: IRS reminder: no itemizing needed to deduct up to $1,000 in charity gifts for 2026
items.caption: Starting with 2026 returns filed next year, standard-deduction filers can deduct cash gifts to charity. Couples get up to $2,000.

visual.foot: Permanent under the Working Families Tax Cuts law

detail: The IRS is reminding taxpayers that a permanent charity deduction for people who don't itemize begins with tax year 2026. Singles can deduct up to $1,000 of cash gifts, and married couples filing jointly up to $2,000.

Only cash gifts to qualified charities count. Donated goods, gifts to donor-advised funds and gifts to supporting organizations don't qualify. Keep receipts, bank records or a letter from the charity showing its name, the date and the amount.
money: Planning year-end giving? Gifts made by Dec. 31 count for your 2026 return.

Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said the economy is growing and hiring has stabilized, so inflation is now his main guide. Kansas City Fed President Jeffrey Schmid also said inflation is running too hot.
The Fed's benchmark rate sits at 3.75% to 4.00% after a September hike. Markets widely expect another quarter-point increase at the Dec. 8-9 meeting, and some expect one more in January.

items.headline: ULA's Vulcan rocket fails for the first time, destroying 40 Amazon Leo satellites
items.caption: The rocket hit trouble about 10 minutes after launch from Cape Canaveral. It is ULA's first total failure since 2006 and a setback for Amazon's satellite internet plans.

visual.title: Amazon Leo setback

detail: United Launch Alliance's Vulcan lifted off Sunday at 12:40 p.m. EST and suffered an anomaly about 10 minutes into flight, failing to reach orbit. Early telemetry suggested problems around the upper stage's burn, but the cause is not yet public.
It was Vulcan's first flight in nine months and ULA's first outright rocket failure since the company formed in 2006. A long grounding is possible.
Amazon has booked 38 Vulcan launches plus flights on Blue Origin's New Glenn, Ariane 6 and SpaceX's Falcon 9. New Glenn is also still waiting to return to flight after a May pad explosion.
money: Delays to Amazon Leo could slow new competition for home internet; don't cancel a current plan expecting a cheap satellite option soon.

risk: The cause is unknown, so the length of any grounding is uncertain.

items.headline: Feds sue Arkansas and Louisiana to protect Kalshi and other prediction markets
items.caption: The DOJ and CFTC say federal law, not state gambling law, governs these markets. Louisiana got a court order covering 31 firms, including Coinbase and Robinhood.

items.st: Seeks to block AG's Kalshi case

detail: The Justice Department and the CFTC sued Arkansas Attorney General Tim Griffin to stop his Nov. 4 lawsuit against Kalshi. They argue the Commodity Exchange Act gives the CFTC exclusive power over regulated event contracts.

In Louisiana, a state judge signed a temporary order requiring 31 companies, including Kalshi, Polymarket, Coinbase, Robinhood and Crypto.com, to stop offering event contracts to residents without a state license. The CFTC sued Louisiana the next day.
Louisiana is the 12th state the CFTC has sued. Kalshi has cut off Louisiana users, and a hearing is set for Nov. 30.
money: If you use prediction markets, your access can change overnight based on where you live; don't leave large balances parked there.
Winnings from event contracts are generally taxable; keep records for tax time.
Brokers like Robinhood and Coinbase face legal costs here; investors in those stocks may see headline risk.
risk: Courts are split, and rulings could quickly expand or shrink where these markets operate.
Treat event contracts as speculation; you can lose your whole stake.

items.headline: About 32,000 people could lose Medicare on Feb. 1 under new immigrant eligibility rules
items.caption: Social Security sent notices Nov. 10 to enrollees whose immigration status it can't confirm. US citizens and green card holders are not affected.
detail: The Social Security Administration sent notices on Nov. 10 saying some Medicare enrollees could lose coverage Feb. 1, 2027, unless they prove their immigration status by the deadline in their letter. CMS estimates about 32,000 people are affected.

The change comes from the July 2025 tax and spending law, which removed refugees, asylum grantees, TPS holders and others from Medicare eligibility. Green card holders, Cuban-Haitian entrants and certain Pacific Island migrants remain eligible. More than 70 million people are on Medicare.

items.headline: Family of a Houston man hit by an ICE vehicle says it was intentional
items.caption: A Texas grand jury indicted the ICE officer on aggravated assault. ICE says the man ran in front of the vehicle and calls the prosecution a political stunt.

items.t: Lawmakers write to ICE and DHS

detail: Miguel Parra Hernandez, 48, a construction worker who has lived in the U.S. for 34 years, was struck by an ICE vehicle in Houston on Oct. 10. Video shows him running before the vehicle hits him from behind. He was not the target of the operation and remains in ICE custody.

A Harris County grand jury indicted ICE officer Mario Alberto Morales on a felony aggravated assault charge. The officer's lawyer calls it an accident. ICE says Parra Hernandez ran in front of the vehicle and calls the case a political stunt.

ICE does not dispute that he has no criminal record but says he is in the country illegally. His siblings told CBS News the act was intentional. House Democrats led by Rep. Lizzie Fletcher accused ICE of limiting family and lawyer access.
money: Detention can wipe out a household's income overnight. Families should know where key papers and bank access are kept.
Construction and other labor-heavy fields may face worker shortages and higher costs as enforcement continues.
For immigration questions, a licensed attorney or accredited representative is worth the cost over a notario.
risk: The criminal case is in early stages; facts are disputed.
Outcomes may shape how state prosecutors handle federal agents.

detail: Plainclothes ICE agents detained Agustin Baccega and Gustavo Romanello, a married couple who work as acrobats, at Phoenix Sky Harbor Airport last weekend. They came to the U.S. on visas in 2020 and soon applied for asylum. Those cases are still pending.

ICE called it a targeted action and said both overstayed their visas. A spokesperson said a pending application or work permit does not give legal status. ICE would not say how agents knew the men would be there.

Their Phoenix lawyer, in practice 17 years, says arrests of people with similar profiles and at airports have risen sharply this year. The airport says it is not told about federal enforcement and doesn't get passenger data.

Detention can halt a paycheck fast. Keep an emergency fund and give a trusted person access if you can.
Low-cost help exists through nonprofits and accredited representatives. Check before paying a notario.
risk: No official count of airport arrests was given.

items.headline: Biotech whiplash: Summit sinks ~20% on an FDA rejection; Helus jumps 23% before data

detail: Summit Therapeutics said Sunday the FDA sent a Complete Response Letter, meaning its application for ivonescimab can't be approved as filed. The drug was meant for advanced EGFR-mutated lung cancer after earlier targeted treatment.

The FDA said a progression-free survival gain alone was not enough without a statistically significant overall survival benefit. Summit's HARMONi trial hit its PFS goal but its survival result only trended positive. Summit says it will keep running other late-stage trials.
On the flip side, Helus Pharma rose more than 23% overnight before topline Phase 3 results for its depression drug HLP003, set for Monday.

items.headline: Supreme Court takes a Robinhood IPO case that could reshape investor lawsuits
items.caption: Justices will decide if a company can be sued for leaving out interim numbers without a misleading statement. Robinhood's 2021 IPO is the test case.
detail: The Supreme Court agreed Friday to hear Robinhood Markets v. Sodha. Investors sued because Robinhood's July 2021 IPO did not include some interim financial data that wasn't due until August 2021.

detail: The IRS warns criminals use stolen Social Security numbers to file fake returns and grab refunds. An IP PIN stops that, because a return using your SSN needs the code.
The online IP PIN system goes offline for maintenance in mid-November and usually returns in mid-January. If you plan to file early in 2027, request it before the shutdown.
If the IRS flags your return, it may hold your refund until you verify your identity.
money: An IP PIN can prevent a stolen refund and months of delays.
Protect your IRS online account with a strong, unique password.

detail: Nebraska began Medicaid work requirements on May 1, months ahead of most states. Adults must log 80 hours a month of work or similar activity unless exempt. The state says 93% of existing enrollees kept coverage.

items.headline: Democrats eye the Social Security tax cap: high earners could pay $6,700 more
items.caption: Sanders wants to lift the payroll tax cap, now $184,500. Raising it to $300,000 would cost someone earning that much about $6,700 a year.

visual.title: Max employee Social Security tax
visual.foot: Employee share at 6.2%. Not law; Congress hasn't voted.

detail: Social Security tax is 6.2% for workers, matched by employers, but only on wages up to a cap. The cap is $184,500 this year and $192,300 in 2027. Sen. Bernie Sanders says lifting it and raising benefits $2,400 a year are top goals now that Democrats will control Congress.

A Tax Policy Center economist estimated a $300,000 cap would cost a worker at that pay about $6,700 more a year. People earning $150,000 would see no change. Removing the cap would close about 58% of the program's long-term gap.
money: If you earn above the cap, watch this debate when planning bonuses, raises or job offers.
Self-employed high earners pay both halves, so a change would hit them twice as hard; plan estimated taxes accordingly.
Retirement income like IRA withdrawals isn't hit by payroll tax, so this mainly affects wages.
risk: Nothing has passed, and the president could veto changes.

Review your return line by line before you sign; you're liable for errors even if a pro filed it.
Keep your own records of income and deductions so you can catch mistakes.
